question: Do the statistical errors catalogued matter, and what changes in education, publishing and practice would reduce them?

results.claim: Schoenfeld and Ioannidis found 216 studies linking 40 of 50 cookbook ingredients to cancer; most disagreed and meta-analyses showed smaller effects.
Of 363 NEJM articles (2001-2010) testing a current practice, 146 (about 40%) concluded it should be abandoned.
Students in 14 physics courses (2,084 students) filled only 23% of the gaps in their knowledge by semester end.
Only 13% of students answered a hypothesis-testing questionnaire correctly even after reading a warning article.
results.setup: Students after an article warning against p value misreadings.

results.claim: Peer instruction fills 50% to 75% of knowledge gaps in physics courses, versus 23% for lectures.

limits: No data of its own; figures come from unprinted endnotes
Peer-instruction evidence is from physics, little exists for statistics (author concedes)
Journal policy descriptions (Nature checklist, Psychological Science) date from 2013-2014
practices: Plan analyses in advance and talk to a statistician before collecting data (p.128)
When reading papers check power or sample size method, variable selection, effect sizes with confidence intervals, multiple-comparison corrections, stopping rules (p.128)
Consult a statistician as a collaborator, not as a replacement for Excel (p.128)

terms.definition: Judging an article by its own views and citations rather than journal prestige.

lineage.work: Ioannidis, Why Most Published Research Findings Are False
lineage.note: mathematical argument from power, bias and low prior odds
